name: growth-default
label: Stress-driven growth law of the remodeling layer (M5 plan, Task 5.7, Deviation 3)
equation: F = Fe Fg, Fg = I + eps_g (Rodriguez, Hoger & McCulloch 1994); d eps_g / dt = r * D, D = Pt (sigma - h sigma_IOP) Pt / s_IOP, with sigma the Cauchy stress, Pt = I - n n^T the projection on the tangent plane of the outer surface, sigma_IOP the stress of the IOP-only eye at the reference age, s_IOP = tr(Pt sigma_IOP Pt) / 2 the local membrane stress under IOP, r the rate (per year), and h the homeostatic ratio. Energy per reference volume Jg W(F Fg^-1). Option (M6 plan, Task 6.6; off by default, see thickness): d eps_g / dt = r * (D + kappa tr(D)/2 n n^T), n the outer surface's normal.

ratePerYear.citation: assumption: no excerpt gave a human scleral or corneal growth rate (search 2026-10-29: Grytz & Siegwart 2015 and Grytz & El Hamdaoui 2017 model tree-shrew scleral remodeling over days; rates not in the excerpts). The local stress feedback of growth, in-plane tangent modulus over s_IOP, is about 800 (sclera), 1700 (limbus), and 2600 (cornea) in the fixture eye under IOP (medians; up to 8600), so r = 0.001 per year gives local time constants under a year; the structural feedback the reduced model computes is smaller, because growth is partly accommodated by deformation. A calibration parameter with wide bounds (data/calibration/priors.json).

homeostaticRatio.citation: assumption: h = 1 makes the pressurized eye of the reference age homeostatic by construction, so only the muscle, lid, and ciliary loads drive growth; h != 1 adds a uniform drive (globe growth or shrinkage). A calibration parameter.

thickness.citation: form: none, the in-plane law the response library and the calibration are validated with. The option form = stress adds growth through the thickness driven by the mean in-plane stress deviation (the shell thickens where its membrane stress exceeds the target, the form in which wall thickness restores wall stress in stress-modulated growth models of arteries; general modeling form, no source transcribed), with kappa the ratio of thickness to in-plane growth rate, an assumption chosen for stability, not measured. Measured on the coarse library (n_face 6, M6 plan, Outcome notes, Task 6.6): with in-plane growth the spherical mode grows at all four tabled stiffness scales (+0.67 to +1.03 per unit r·t); an isochoric constraint makes it worse (+3.13, three growing modes); kappa = 1 (isotropic growth) leaves it marginal (-0.06 to -0.55); kappa = 2 makes it restoring at every scale (-1.15 to -1.79). It is not the default because explicit FEM growth still inverts an element at the edge of the clamped optic-nerve cap at r·t = 0.011 with either law, so it does not extend the validated exposure, and at r·t = 0.01 the reduced model follows the FEM's M within 10.8% with kappa = 2 against 8.4% without.

maxStepFraction.citation: numerical: an explicit growth step is refused (FEM) or sub-stepped (reduced model) when r dt lambda exceeds this, lambda the largest local feedback estimate (in-plane tangent modulus over s_IOP), so no trajectory oscillates or diverges from the step size.

growthStartAgeYears.citation: assumption (approximation): the lid, muscle, and ciliary loads drive growth from birth, so a trajectory that starts at a later baseline age (the calibration's 6 years) begins with the growth amplitudes that this history leaves, not with zero amplitudes; between birth and the baseline age the intensities and the stiffness are held at their baseline-age values, because the loading of infancy is not modeled. Starting from zero at the baseline age instead makes the fast growth modes settle in the first year after it, a transient of the starting state rather than of the mechanism (M5 review, round 1).

fiberReorientation: none (approximation: fiber directions do not turn with growth; small strains)
citation: Rodriguez EK, Hoger A, McCulloch AD, Stress-dependent finite growth in soft elastic tissues, J Biomech 27:455-467, 1994 (the multiplicative decomposition; search excerpt). In-plane tensorial growth with the tissue's in-plane fiber dispersion stands in for the fiber-aligned growth of Grytz & Meschke 2010 (approximation).
